passage: I'm Gopika, and I sit two rows behind Madhav in Class 10. On Tuesday, Mr Kurian read out his test mark and said, "Maybe try opening a book this year." A few people laughed. I saw Madhav's neck go red, his jaw working, his fingers digging into the desk edge. He stood up so fast his chair scraped. I honestly thought he would shout something he couldn't take back. Instead he said, in a tight voice, "May I go to the washroom, sir?" and walked out. Through the window I saw him at the tap, splashing cold water on his face again and again. When he came back, his shoulders were down. After class he went up to Mr Kurian and said calmly, "That comment hurt. Can we talk about my marks another time?" I don't know what was going on in his head, but I know what he didn't say.

qa.q: What did Madhav do at the tap?
qa.a: Madhav was splashing cold water on his face again and again.

qa.q: What might Madhav's red neck and digging fingers suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: They suggest Madhav was flooded with anger and humiliation after the comment, though Gopika could not know for sure.

qa.q: Which choice did Madhav make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Madhav left for the washroom and cooled down with water before speaking, so he could raise the hurt calmly instead of saying something he couldn't take back.

qa.q: How might Mr Kurian have felt when Madhav said calmly that the comment hurt?
qa.a: Mr Kurian may have felt caught off guard and perhaps sorry, since a calm complaint is harder to dismiss than an outburst.

grounding: A teenager provoked by a teacher is visibly flooded with anger, steps out and uses cold water so the surge falls before speaking.

passage:
Monday. When his younger sister Madhuri read his message to a friend out loud at dinner, Tenzin's face burned and his pulse thudded in his ears. "You're a pathetic little snoop and nobody likes you!" he yelled. Madhuri's face crumpled. He lay awake that night wishing he could take it back.
Thursday. She grabbed his phone again, laughing. The same heat rushed up his neck; the room seemed to shrink to her grinning face. Tenzin put the phone down, said, "I'm going for a run," and pounded around the colony twice until his breath came back.
Saturday. Tenzin knocked on her door. "What I said on Monday was cruel. I'm sorry. But reading my stuff isn't okay." Madhuri nodded, eyes down. "I know. Sorry."

qa.q: What did Tenzin do on Thursday when the heat rushed up his neck?
qa.a: Tenzin said he was going for a run and pounded around the colony twice.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling the night after Monday's dinner?
qa.a: Tenzin felt regret and guilt, lying awake wishing he could take back what he yelled.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Thursday, and why did it help?
qa.a: On Thursday Tenzin noticed the rising heat and left for a run before speaking, so the anger dropped and he could apologise and set a limit calmly on Saturday.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have felt when Tenzin yelled on Monday?
qa.a: Madhuri was hurt; her face crumpled when she was called a pathetic snoop.

grounding: A teenager's heat, pounding pulse and narrowed focus lead to cruel words, and next time he steps away for a run before speaking.

passage: Ada was reading Kwame's message to Efua out loud to her friends in the Accra kitchen, in a silly voice. Kwame's face burned. His pulse was thudding in his ears, and all he could see was his sister's grinning face, as if the rest of the room had gone dark. He had the words ready, the cruelest thing he knew about her and her failed exam. He opened his mouth. Then he turned around and walked out of the gate. He ran, hard, to the end of the road and back, twice. His lungs hurt. The heat drained slowly out of his face. When he came back in, Ada was alone. 'That was really not okay,' he said, his voice steady. 'Give me my phone.' She looked at the floor. 'Sorry. It was stupid.'

qa.q: Who was Ada reading the message to?
qa.a: Her friends.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling while Ada read his message aloud?
qa.a: He was humiliated and furious, with a burning face, thudding pulse and eyes locked on Ada.

qa.q: Why was running to the end of the road a good choice?
qa.a: It let the surge of anger fall so Kwame could speak steadily instead of saying something cruel he could not take back.

qa.q: How might Ada have felt when Kwame came back calm?
qa.a: She was probably ashamed and a little surprised, which made it easier for her to apologise.

grounding: Shows a teenager provoked by a sibling, feeling heat, a pounding pulse and tunnel vision, who runs to let the surge fall before speaking.

passage: In the chemistry lab, Sahil Sir held up Devika's practical file. 'Copied from Tanya, obviously. Same mistakes.' The class turned to look. Devika's face flamed. Her pulse pounded so hard she could barely hear. All she could see was his hand holding her file. She had worked till midnight on it. Words rushed up her throat, sharp and loud. She gripped the bench. 'Sir, may I go to the washroom?' He waved her out. At the tap she splashed cold water on her face and wrists again and again, breathing out slowly. After five minutes her heartbeat had eased. After class she went to his desk. 'Sir, I didn't copy. Tanya and I studied together, so we made the same mistake. Can I show you my rough work?' He paused. 'Bring it tomorrow.'

qa.q: What did Devika splash on her face and wrists?
qa.a: Cold water.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when Sahil Sir held up her file?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and furious at being accused unfairly in front of the class.

qa.q: What helped Devika speak calmly later?
qa.a: Leaving the lab, splashing cold water and breathing slowly until her heartbeat eased.

qa.q: How might Sahil Sir see things after Devika's calm explanation?
qa.a: He may be more willing to consider that he was wrong, since she spoke respectfully and offered evidence.

grounding: Shows a teenager provoked by a teacher, feeling heat, pounding pulse and tunnel vision, who uses cold water and time away to let the surge fall before speaking.

passage:
Samir,
I'm writing this because I don't trust my voice yet. Yesterday, when I saw my headphones snapped in half on your bed, I went hot all over. My heart was banging in my ears. I could only see those broken headphones. I had words ready that I know would have hurt you for a long time. Things about you being useless. I'm glad I didn't say them.
Instead, I went out and ran around the colony till my legs burned. When I came back, I still felt angry, but not like I'd explode.
I'm still upset. Those headphones were my birthday present. But I want to talk about it properly, not shout. Can we talk after dinner tonight? You can tell me what happened.
Your brother,
Santosh

qa.q: What did Santosh find snapped in half?
qa.a: The headphones.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he saw the broken headphones?
qa.a: Santosh was furious, hot all over, with a heart banging and only the broken headphones in view.

qa.q: What did Santosh do instead of saying the hurtful words?
qa.a: He ran around the colony till his legs burned, then wrote to Samir to talk calmly.

qa.q: How might Samir feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Samir may feel guilty but relieved that Santosh did not shout, and more ready to talk honestly.

grounding: Shows a teenager provoked by a sibling, feeling heat and tunnel vision, who runs to let the anger fall before speaking.

passage: Madhav, you saw me walk out of chemistry today, right? Let me, Irawati, explain before the rumours start. When Mr Kulkarni called me careless in front of the whole class, after I'd stayed up finishing that practical, something just exploded inside. My face burned, my heart hammered in my ears, and I could only see his face, like looking down a tunnel. I had words ready that I could never take back. So I asked to go to the washroom and walked out. I splashed cold water on my face, held my wrists under the tap and walked two laps of the ground. By the second lap the fire had gone down. Then I went back and asked to talk to him after class. Calmly.

qa.q: What did Irawati do at the tap?
qa.a: Splashed cold water on the face and held the wrists under the tap.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when Mr Kulkarni called the work careless?
qa.a: Irawati felt a surge of rage, face burning, heart hammering and vision narrowed like a tunnel.

qa.q: Why was walking out a wise move?
qa.a: Stepping away with cold water and two laps let the surge fall before any words were said that couldn't be taken back.

qa.q: How might Madhav and the class have seen Irawati walking out?
qa.a: They might have thought Irawati was being rude or dramatic, not knowing it was a way to avoid saying something hurtful.

grounding: A provoked teenager feels heat, a pounding pulse and tunnel vision, and steps away with cold water and a walk before speaking.
